The retail decision · Data to decisions

Recommend the next phase of expansion.

Use the evidence accumulated through the ten lessons to advise the operations director.

The recommendation

Continue a measured expansion of replenishment alerts in stores comparable to the later rollout group. Use the forecast to organize the weekly review workload, retain a comparison during expansion, and track both stockout rates and the cost of delivering the service.

The operational case is a persistent stockout burden above the 10% target. The intervention studies point to improved availability, while their economic results depend on the target store mix and the stated accounting costs. The pilot’s saving interval reaches slightly below zero, so a staged commitment remains useful.

What established the need for action

Lesson 1 reconciled 1,200 store-weeks and established a baseline rate of 12.74%. Lesson 2 showed how that burden differed across delivery groups. The independent week-16 audit estimated 11.50%, with interval 10.22%–12.78%.

These are complementary observations of the same business at named times. They justify attention to replenishment and preserve a stable definition for measuring progress.

How the analysis supports daily work

Lessons 4 and 5 made the relationship between store conditions and stockout pressure explicit. Lesson 6 selected Linear regression using later validation weeks and recorded final forecast error of 2.96 points, versus 3.88 for the mean-rate rule.

The review queue should be formed before the week starts. Record staff actions and effort so the company can distinguish a useful forecast from an effective operational response.

What the intervention evidence says

Three studies of the same policy, with named targets
Study and targetEstimated reduction (points)95% intervalAccounting saving (CU/store-week)
Randomized pilot: 50 eligible pilot stores3.492.36 to 4.629.28
Voluntary cohort: adjusted all-store target3.012.39 to 3.63Model implication: 5.27
Later rollout: selected adopter stores4.593.92 to 5.2518.52

The randomized pilot estimates the offer’s effect for its pilot population. The adjusted voluntary result uses recorded starting conditions to represent all stores in that cohort. The time comparison evaluates the selected later adopters. Their store mixes differ, so they should not be averaged automatically into a universal effect.

Make the break-even point visible

Break-even reduction=208.4=2.38 percentage points

The pilot’s estimated weekly saving is 9.28 CU, with interval -0.22 to 18.78. The later-rollout saving is 18.52 CU, with interval 12.91 to 24.13.

These savings use the supplied 6 CU stockout charge and 20 CU policy cost. Before committing a budget, finance should agree whether that accounting rule represents the business objective and update it if service fees or carrying costs change.

Specify what the next phase will record

Name the eligible stores, offer date, common monitoring basket, and follow-up window before expansion. Preserve the weekly stockout denominator and identify which stores provide the comparison. Record the alert service actually delivered, review effort, inventory costs, and other operational changes.

Set the review date and decision rule in advance: continue where the service improvement and cost case support it; revise the operating protocol where implementation absorbs the gain. The next analysis should update this memo using the same store IDs and explicit targets.

Write your own board paragraph

In one paragraph, name the target stores, the evidence you rely on, the expected improvement in business units, the cost rule, and the next action. Then explain which new result would change your recommendation.

Compare with a possible response

Approve a staged next phase for stores resembling the selected rollout adopters. The time comparison estimates a meaningful reduction in stockouts with positive accounting savings under the supplied cost rule. Retain a contemporaneous comparison and audit delivery of the alert service. Use the pilot’s less precise financial result to avoid assuming the same payoff at every store. Review both availability and operating costs at the pre-specified decision date.

Capstone: make and defend your own decision

The recommendation above is one worked response, not the required answer. Prepare a two-page memo plus a reproducible appendix. Compare three feasible options: retain usual operations while gathering more evidence; expand to a defined comparable subset; or run a randomized next phase before broader commitment. Do not average estimates from different study populations into one universal effect.

Planning scenario: the next phase has 30 eligible stores and staff can conduct five additional reviews each week. These capacity figures are exercise assumptions, not facts established by the case. State whether your intervention can be delivered within that constraint. A forecast review queue and the weekly alert service are distinct activities; document the workload and cost of each rather than treating the five-slot queue as permission to treat 30 stores.

A one-point reduction avoids 1.4 stockout product-days per store-week because exposure is 140. At the rollout point estimate, the least favorable displayed accounting scenario can reverse the financial recommendation. Repeat the cost calculation at the study interval endpoints, while recognizing that those endpoints do not quantify bias from a violated trend assumption or uncertain accounting values.

Your analysis appendix must show the selected study target, effect and interval; a matching balance assessment where relevant; the capacity-matched forecast check; and at least one scenario involving missing data, an unmeasured common cause or an unequal untreated trend. Explain why your recommendation follows even after considering that scenario—or explain why it no longer follows.

Predeclare an evaluation plan: eligible units, assignment/comparison, primary outcome, worthwhile improvement, sample-size assumptions, follow-up, implementation records, missing-outcome procedure and review date. Describe a result that would trigger continuation, revision or stopping. Separate a threshold chosen for teaching from an operating commitment that would require management agreement.

20-point rubric: 0 absent; 1 named; 2 partly supported; 3 substantially supported; 4 complete and coherent
CriterionPointsEvidence for full credit
Measurement and target4Correct units, denominators, time periods, coverage and eligible population
Design and identification4Assignment/trend/control assumptions and plausible failure mechanisms
Calculation and uncertainty4Reproducible contrasts, matched targets, appropriate intervals and sensitivity
Operations and economics4Capacity, costs, benefits, alternatives and a feasible implementation protocol
Judgment and communication4A defensible choice, material limits and a specific result that would reverse it

Assess the reasoning, not agreement with the worked recommendation. A proposal to delay, gather better comparison data or narrow the target can earn full credit. A numerical estimate with the wrong population or an unsupported causal claim cannot be rescued by polished presentation.

Transfer challenge: repeat the decision structure for a staff-training program with incomplete attendance and shared managers. Describe what replaces the stockout denominator, why assignment and receipt differ, which unit should be randomized, and what outcome and cost records are needed. Do not reuse the retail effect size as evidence for training.
